function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m happy to help you set up the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow for the **nodejs-welcome** repository.  
Below are step‑by‑step instructions and the content you’ll need to add to the repo.  

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you don’t have SSH keys set up, you can clone via HTTPS instead:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Create Required Files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Assuming the repo contains a simple Node.js application (e.g., `app.js` or `index.js`) that listens on port **3000**, here’s a minimal Dockerfile:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and suitable for production.  
> * `npm ci` ensures a clean install of production dependencies.  
> * The app is started with `node app.js` – adjust if your entry point differs.

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a file named `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can create a `k8s` folder if it doesn’t exist):

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does:**  
> * Deploys two replicas of your Node.js app.  
> * Exposes the app internally via a ClusterIP service on port 80, mapping to container port 3000.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Node.js
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      # Install dependencies
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      # Run tests (if any)
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      # Build Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker tag zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

      # Push Docker image to Docker Hub (optional)
      # Uncomment and configure if you want to push
      # - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      #   uses: docker/login-action@v2
      #   with:
      #     username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
      #     password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

      # - name: Push Docker image
      #   run: |
      #     docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
      #     docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What this workflow does:**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Installs Node.js, installs dependencies, runs tests, builds a Docker image, and tags it.  
> * Optionally pushes the image to Docker Hub if you set up the secrets.

---

## 3️⃣ Add, Commit, and Push Changes

```bash
# Stage the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# Commit the changes
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the remote repository
git push origin main
```

> **Note:**  
> * Ensure you have write access to the repository.  
> * If you’re using SSH, make sure your SSH key is added to your GitHub account.  
> * If you’re using HTTPS, you may need to provide your credentials or a personal access token.

---

### Recap

1. **Clone** the repo locally.  
2. **Create** the Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, and GitHub Actions workflow as shown above.  
3. **Stage**, **commit**, and **push** the changes back to GitHub.

Let me know if you’d like help with any specific part of this process!
